Recommendations on how an NSO can approach retailers to acquire scanner
data\

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Initial steps in the acquisition of scanner data {#Initialstepsintheacquisitionofscannerdata-Initialstepsintheacquisitionofscannerdata}

Once the retailers that fit the [sample purposes of the Consumer Price
Index (CPI) are
identified](selection-of-retailers-for-alternative-data-sources.qmd),
the National Statistical Office (NSO) needs to approach data owners to
negotiate data acquisition. As stated in the reference guides
Eurostat\'s HICP - [Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner
Data](https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/7b031f10-ac19-4da3-a36f-58708a70133d/library/8e1333df-ca16-40fc-bc6a-1ce1be37247c/details)
and the [CPI Manual, Concepts and
Methods](https://www.imf.org/-/media/Files/Data/CPI/cpi-manual-concepts-and-methods.ashx),
2020, the most recommended practice is to negotiate and get the data
directly from the retailers. This approach encompasses advantages such
as the possibility to negotiate a data supply at reduced costs (or even
free), and to discuss with the retailers the data requirements desired
in terms of data content that should be provided, and timetables that
agree with CPI production routines.

As scanner data contains valuable sensitive information of the retailers
and the ongoing data supply involves extra costs as the implementation
and maintenance of an IT structure, retailers might be reluctant to
provide the information to the NSOs and can require funds for their
extra costs (Ref. (1)). The existence of legislation that allows the NSO
the right to get access to the data can support any access requests but
discussions are still required to ensure the data provided meet the
requirements of the NSO.

Previous experiences show that negotiations with retailers to get
scanner data can take several months. This can include the following
steps:

1.  Identifying suitable contacts within the retailer to take forward
    the request. Generally, you will need to work with the retailer\'s
    data team on the specific requirements and data access, but it is
    likely you will also need to gain approval from higher level
    decision makers within the retailer to progress the project, and the
    retailer\'s legal team may also need to sign off any data sharing
    agreements or contracts that are put in place.
2.  Agreeing a data transfer method. There are many methods available,
    from using secure encryption email services to cloud sharing
    technologies such as Amazon S3 buckets.
3.  Agreeing a data specification. This is likely to require a few
    iterations from receiving an initial test data set, resolving any
    outstanding queries or requirements and finalising the format and
    shape of the desired output.
4.  Agreeing a frequency of delivery. This is likely to include the
    regular feeds but also any historic data that the retailer can
    provide.
5.  Finalising these agreements in a data sharing agreement or contract.

Some NSOs have a separate commercial data acquisition team that work on
behalf of the whole office to acquire administrative data. It is helpful
to have a clear point of contact within the NSO and maintain a high
level of engagement to ensure negotiations remain on track. To identify
suitable contacts within the retailer it is sometimes easier to target
high-level company managers to ensure a suitable priority is given to
this work. The discussions on data content are then generally delegated
to a specific data team within the retailer. The retailers are also
likely to have separate legal teams that will need to be involved when
agreeing the terms of the data sharing agreements.  

A key point for the success of the approach relies on the NSO building
and maintaining a good relationship with the retailers ([Practical Guide
for Processing Supermarket Scanner
Data](https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/7b031f10-ac19-4da3-a36f-58708a70133d/library/8e1333df-ca16-40fc-bc6a-1ce1be37247c/details)).
A clear argument for the statistical purpose of accessing the data and
the relevance of the results produced for the society are important
points to present. The benefits for the retailers should also be
emphasized. The response burden is lowered by the adoption of scanner
data since the staff of the retailers will no longer need to reply to
the collectors\' questions nor be bothered by the collectors walking
around in the stores every month. Some NSOs also provide opportunities
for collaboration with the retailer (ensuring this does not lead to a
specific competitive advantage), for example providing specific retailer
prices indices back to the retailer. 

In the training course 2 about data acquisition, in [module
2.1](https://unstats.un.org/wiki/display/GWGSD/Training+material#Trainingmaterial-Module2.1:AcquiringscannerdataforCPI(inprogress):~:text=with%20voice%20over-,2.%20Data%20acquisition,-Pre%2Drequisite%3A%20None)
a general description of the process to arrive at obtaining scanner data
is traced in the form of a decision three.

Readers can also find a list of recommendations for obtaining scanner
data in section 5 of Eurostat\'s [Practical Guide for Processing
Supermarket Scanner
Data](https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/7b031f10-ac19-4da3-a36f-58708a70133d/library/8e1333df-ca16-40fc-bc6a-1ce1be37247c/details).
